steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our measurement paper on how Consent Management Platforms have spread over the years and how users interact with privacy banners. Give the background on ad tracking and privacy laws, describe our two datasets and main findings, mention limitations, and give the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Web advertising, IBA and third-party cookies
2. Regulation: Cookie Law, GDPR and laws elsewhere
3. CMPs as outsourced banner management
4. Our study: system view (HTTP Archive) and user view (illow.io)
5. Main findings: CMP growth and cookie behavior; user choices
6. Dataset limitations, data release, paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Ads and tracking
- many websites earn revenue from ads; Web intertwined with people's lives
- Interest-Based Advertisement (IBA): users more interested in ads matching their interests -> per-user profiles
- third-party (profiling) cookies at center; third party sees visits on sites where it is present -> navigation history, interests

2. Regulation
- privacy concerns -> legislators regulate, raise user awareness
- EU "Cookie Law" 2009: approval via Privacy Banner for first- or third-party cookies
- GDPR 2018: severe fines
- elsewhere: CCPA (California) 2018, Brazil LGPD, Canada PIPEDA 2000 (being reformed)
- Privacy Banners pervasive

3. CMPs
- avoid burden of creating/controlling/checking compliance with evolving rules -> outsource
- CMPs handle technical complexity; simple mechanism for consent and data collection

4. Study
- longitudinal measurement; two angles: system and end user
- system: global CMP evolution, growth, market share, effectiveness at controlling third-party cookies, geographic spread; HTTP Archive, millions of websites since 2015
- user: medium-sized CMP illow.io; effect of one-click-choice option, banner position, device, country; more than two years, more than 20 million interactions

5. Findings
- GDPR and similar laws -> CMP explosion, 40% of websites in Europe
- more websites removing third-party tracking entirely
- more than 50% of CMP websites still install third-party cookies before acceptance; complexity, no standard enforcement
- websites must adapt per regulation and country -> need more analysis, archival projects
- users: more than 60% deny with one-click reject-all; mostly to dismiss banner, not conscious decision
- where opt-out needs more than one click, about 90% accept via one-click accept-all
- iOS users accept more than Android; maybe higher confidence in privacy on Apple devices

6. Limitations / outline
- neither dataset collected for this work; opportunistic
- HTTP Archive only U.S. locations; limiting as Web customized by location
- publish pre-processed HTTP Archive dataset + figure code
- Sec 2 regulation history + related work; Sec 3 methodology/datasets; Sec 4 CMP pervasiveness; Sec 5 user interactions with illow.io; Sec 6 summary

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Web advertising has kept evolving, since the Web is more and more part of people's lives and many websites get their revenue from advertisements (ads). To make ads more effective, Interest-Based Advertisement (IBA) starts from the assumption that users will be more interested in ads that are about their specific interests. On the Web this led to mechanisms that build specific profiles for each user, so IBA can be very detailed. Third-party cookies have been at the center of the IBA ecosystem. Once these profiling cookies are installed in the user's browser, they let a third party collect information on the visits the user makes to websites where the third party is present. In this way the third party learns the user's navigation history and can work out what they are interested in.

Over the years cookies raised privacy concerns for users, and legislators started to regulate the abuse of these practices on the Web and to make users more aware of the process. In the European Union, the first big step was the "Cookie Law" in 2009. It says that every website using first- or third-party cookies has to get the user's approval through a Privacy Banner. This was enforced further in 2018 with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which brought severe fines for websites and organizations that do not comply. Other legislators around the world also started regulating the collection of personal data, so Privacy Banners are now everywhere, as we all see when surfing the Web. For example, there is California's California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in 2018, the Brazilian General Personal Data Protection Law (LGPD), and the Canadian Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) in 2000, which is currently being reformed.

Creating Privacy Banners, controlling them and checking that they comply with existing and changing regulations is a burden, so websites often outsource banner creation and management to external companies that offer Consent Management Platforms (CMPs). CMPs deal with the technical complexity of implementing Privacy Banners and give their customers a simple mechanism to install and manage user consent and data collection in general.

In this paper we present a longitudinal measurement study. We want to understand how the Consent Management Platform landscape has evolved over the years and how users interact with CMPs. We look at it from two angles, the system point of view and the end-user point of view. From the system side, we break down how CMPs evolved globally: the growth of different solutions, their market share, how effective they are at controlling third-party cookies, and how they spread in different geographical regions. For this we use the HTTP Archive, which is a unique opportunity because it has the history of millions of websites since 2015.

- User view:
  - illow.io CMP (medium-sized); one-click-choice option, banner position, device, country
  - more than two years, more than 20 million interactions
- Findings (system):
  - CMPs on 40% of websites in Europe after GDPR and similar laws
  - more sites remove third-party tracking
  - more than 50% install third-party cookies before acceptance (complexity, no standard enforcement)
  - per-country/regulation behavior -> more analysis, archival projects
- Findings (users):
  - more than 60% reject with one-click reject-all, mostly to dismiss banner
  - about 90% accept where opt-out needs more than one click
  - iOS users accept more than Android users
- Limitations: datasets not designed for this work; HTTP Archive U.S.-only; release pre-processed data + code
- Outline: Sections 2-6

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Web advertising has kept evolving, since the Web is more and more part of people's lives and many websites get their revenue from advertisements (ads). To make ads more effective, Interest-Based Advertisement (IBA) starts from the assumption that users will be more interested in ads that are about their specific interests. On the Web this led to mechanisms that build specific profiles for each user, so IBA can be very detailed. Third-party cookies have been at the center of the IBA ecosystem. Once these profiling cookies are installed in the user's browser, they let a third party collect information on the visits the user makes to websites where the third party is present. In this way the third party learns the user's navigation history and can work out what they are interested in.

Over the years cookies raised privacy concerns for users, and legislators started to regulate the abuse of these practices on the Web and to make users more aware of the process. In the European Union, the first big step was the "Cookie Law" in 2009. It says that every website using first- or third-party cookies has to get the user's approval through a Privacy Banner. This was enforced further in 2018 with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which brought severe fines for websites and organizations that do not comply. Other legislators around the world also started regulating the collection of personal data, so Privacy Banners are now everywhere, as we all see when surfing the Web. For example, there is California's California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in 2018, the Brazilian General Personal Data Protection Law (LGPD), and the Canadian Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) in 2000, which is currently being reformed.

Creating Privacy Banners, controlling them and checking that they comply with existing and changing regulations is a burden, so websites often outsource banner creation and management to external companies that offer Consent Management Platforms (CMPs). CMPs deal with the technical complexity of implementing Privacy Banners and give their customers a simple mechanism to install and manage user consent and data collection in general.

In this paper we present a longitudinal measurement study. We want to understand how the Consent Management Platform landscape has evolved over the years and how users interact with CMPs. We look at it from two angles, the system point of view and the end-user point of view. From the system side, we break down how CMPs evolved globally: the growth of different solutions, their market share, how effective they are at controlling third-party cookies, and how they spread in different geographical regions. For this we use the HTTP Archive, which is a unique opportunity because it has the history of millions of websites since 2015.

From the end-user side, we use the preferences users expressed when interacting with a medium-sized CMP. We look at the impact of different options, like whether there is a "one-click-choice" option or not, where the banner is, which device they use, which country they are from, and so on. For this we use a unique dataset from the illow.io CMP, which covers more than two years since it entered the CMP market and has more than 20 million interactions with the CMP.

Our study shows that the GDPR and similar regulations caused an explosion of CMPs, which are now on 40% of websites in Europe. We also see more websites choosing to remove third-party tracking technologies directly, probably weighing the benefit against the complexity of managing them. Surprisingly, more than 50% of websites with a CMP still install third-party cookies of possible tracking services before the user accepts them. This is because managing third-party content is complex and there are no standard technical solutions for CMPs to enforce the user's choice. Also, today a website has to change its behavior with third parties depending on the regulations and the user's country. This calls for more analysis and bigger archival projects.

On the user side, we see that more than 60% of users deny third-party tracking cookies when they are offered a simple "one-click reject-all" action. But most of these choices come from wanting to get the intrusive banner off the screen quickly, not from an explicit and conscious decision. In fact, in countries where opting out needs more than one click, about 90% of users accept cookies with a one-click accept-all button. Curiously, iOS users accept cookies more often than Android users. This may be related to higher confidence in the privacy offered by iOS and Apple devices.

Neither the HTTP Archive nor the illow.io dataset was collected or designed for this work. But because they are available we can study them and present interesting insights in an opportunistic way. In particular, HTTP Archive collects data only from locations in the U.S., and this is a limitation today, because the Web is more and more customized to the user's location to follow the different privacy regulations. So that part of our results can be reproduced, we publish online the pre-processed HTTP Archive dataset and the code to make the figures in this paper.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 introduces the regulation history and related work. Section 3 discusses the methodology and the datasets. Section 4 shows how the pervasiveness of CMPs on the Web has evolved over time, and Section 5 focuses on how users interact with the Privacy Banners of the illow.io CMP. Finally, Section 6 summarizes our main findings.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The landscape of Web advertising has been continuously evolving, since the Web is more and more intertwined with people's lives and many websites base their revenues on advertisements (ads). To maximize ad effectiveness, Interest-Based Advertisement (IBA) builds on the fundamental assumption that users will be more interested in ads related to their specific interests. In the Web ecosystem, this fueled the deployment of mechanisms that build specific per-user profiles, pushing IBA to a great level of detail. Third-party cookies have largely been at the center of the IBA ecosystem. Once installed in the end user's browser, these so-called profiling cookies enable a third party to collect information on the visits a user performs on the websites where the third party is present [1,2,3]. This allows the third party to collect information about the users' navigation history and derive their interests.

Over the years, the use of cookies raised concerns for users' privacy, and legislators started acting to regulate the abuse of these practices across the Web and to increase users' awareness of the process. In the European Union, the first significant step in this direction was the "Cookie Law" [4] in 2009, which states that every website using first- or third-party cookies must obtain the user's approval via a Privacy Banner. The measure was further enforced in 2018 with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [5], which introduced severe fines for non-compliant websites and organizations. Other legislators around the globe similarly started regulating the collection of personal data, making Privacy Banners pervasive, as we all experience while surfing the Web. Notable examples are the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) [6] in 2018, the Brazilian General Personal Data Protection Law (LGPD) [7], and the Canadian Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) [8] in 2000 (currently being reformed [9]).

To avoid the burden of creating, controlling, and checking the compliance of Privacy Banners with existing and evolving regulations, websites often outsource banner creation and management to external companies offering Consent Management Platforms (CMPs). CMPs take care of the technical complexity of implementing Privacy Banners and offer their customers a simple mechanism to install and manage user consent and data collection at large.

In this paper, we present a longitudinal measurement study that aims to understand how the Consent Management Platform landscape has evolved over the years and how users interact with CMPs. We consider two angles: the system point of view and the end-user point of view. From the system point of view, we break down the global evolution of CMPs, observing the growth of different solutions, their market share, their effectiveness in controlling the usage of third-party cookies, and their spread across geographical regions. For this, we leverage the unique opportunity offered by the HTTP Archive [10], which includes the history of millions of websites since 2015.

From the end-user perspective, we leverage the preferences expressed by users interacting with a medium-sized CMP, observing the impact of different options such as the presence (or absence) of a "one-click-choice" option, the position of the banner, the device used, the user's country, etc. To this end, we leverage a unique dataset from the illow.io CMP, which spans more than two years of data since its introduction in the CMP market and contains more than 20 million interactions with the CMP.

Our study reveals that the introduction of the GDPR and similar regulations fuelled the explosion of CMPs, which are now present on 40% of websites in Europe. We also observe an increase in websites that opted to remove third-party tracking technologies directly, probably balancing the benefit against the complexity of managing them. Surprisingly, more than 50% of websites adopting a CMP still install third-party cookies of possible tracking services before the user accepts their usage. This is due to the complexity of managing third-party content and the lack of standard technical solutions for CMPs to enforce the user's choice. Moreover, a website nowadays must adapt its behavior with third parties depending on regulations and on the user's country, which calls for more analysis and more extensive archival projects.

From the user's point of view, we observe that more than 60% of users deny the usage of third-party tracking cookies when offered a simple "one-click reject-all" action. Yet the large majority of these choices stem from the intent to quickly remove the intrusive banner from the screen rather than from an explicit and conscious decision. Indeed, in countries where the opt-out choice requires more than one click, about 90% of users accept cookies via a one-click accept-all button. Curiously, iOS users accept cookies more frequently than Android users, which may be linked to a higher confidence in the privacy offered by iOS and Apple devices.

Neither the HTTP Archive nor the illow.io dataset was collected or designed specifically for this work. Still, their availability allows us to study them and present interesting insights in an opportunistic manner. In particular, HTTP Archive collects its data only from locations in the U.S., which is limiting nowadays, as the Web is increasingly customized based on users' location to adapt to different privacy regulations. To allow the reproducibility of part of our results, we publish online the pre-processed HTTP Archive dataset and the code to obtain the figures of this paper [11].

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the regulation history and discusses related work. Section 3 discusses the methodology and the datasets used in our analysis. Section 4 presents how the pervasiveness of CMPs on the Web has evolved over time, while Section 5 focuses on users' interactions with the Privacy Banners of the illow.io CMP. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the main findings of our work.
